title: Tunable flat band on the surface of a rhombohedral kagome ferromagnet
authors: Xinglu Que, Qingyu He, Lihui Zhou, Lilian Prodan, Vladimir Tsurkan, István Kézsmárki, Hidenori Takagi, Dennis Huang
abstract: A central goal in the exploration of kagome-based materials is the realization of a flat band that has meV bandwidth and lies close to the Fermi energy. The prevailing assumption is that band flattening originates from destructive hopping processes on the kagome lattice. We perform scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) on the layered kagome ferromagnet Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ and show that it indeed hosts a flat band near the Fermi energy, which is manifested as a sharp peak in the differential tunneling conductance. First-principles slab calculations reveal, however, that this band is flattened not by the destructive interference of intralayer hopping, but by interlayer hopping between rhombohedral-stacked kagome planes in Fe$_3$Sn$_2$, and is confined to the surface layer. This surface band, forming in the vicinity of the Brillouin zone corners $\bar{K}$ and $\bar{K'}$, exhibits rich magnetic-field dependence, including fine structure due to valley-symmetry breaking by rotated Fe moments, as well as a persistent diamagnetic shift associated with orbital magnetic moments, all reproduced by our calculations. Our results, highlighting the crucial role of layer stacking on the band structure of kagome magnets, demonstrate experimentally an alternative mechanism of generating magnetically tunable flat bands in atomically thin volumes of topological magnets.
summary: This research investigates flat bands in the kagome ferromagnet $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{Sn}_2$, demonstrating that the band flattening mechanism is governed by interlayer hopping rather than previously assumed intralayer frustration. By combining STM measurements with DFT calculations, the authors reveal that the surface band's properties are highly tunable by external magnetic fields, offering a new pathway to engineer topological electronic states.
main_problem: The central goal is to understand the origin and magnetic tunability of flat electronic bands in kagome-based magnetic materials.
main_result: The flat band is shown to originate not from intralayer hopping frustration, but from interlayer hopping between rhombohedrally stacked planes, and exhibits rich magnetic-field dependence.
method: The study combines Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) measurements with first-principles Density Functional Theory (DFT) slab calculations and a tight-binding (TB) model.
model_or_system: The physical system is the layered kagome ferromagnet $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{Sn}_2$. The analysis focuses on the electronic structure of the surface layer, which is influenced by the rhombohedral stacking sequence and the magnetic ordering of the Fe moments.
key_observables: Sharp peaks in the differential tunneling conductance ($	ext{d}I/	ext{d}V$), exhibiting field-dependent features like valley splitting and diamagnetic shifts.
important_parameters: The magnetic field orientation ($B_{\parallel}$ vs. $B_{\perp}$), the degree of magnetization polarization ($m_{\parallel}$ vs. $m_{\perp}$), and the interlayer hopping strength.
main_assumptions: The initial assumption that flat bands arise from intralayer hopping interference is refuted; the analysis relies on the DFT/STM comparison, which has inherent approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure and stacking (Fig. 1), STM topography and $	ext{d}I/	ext{d}V$ spectra showing peaks $s$ and $s^*$ (Fig. 2, 3), and DFT band structures confirming valley splitting under perpendicular magnetization (Fig. 5).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the existence of the flat band via STM, to theoretically identifying the interlayer hopping mechanism via DFT, and finally detailing the magnetic field dependence and underlying physics using both DFT and a TB model.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, experimentally verified example of how structural details (layer stacking) dictate electronic properties (flat bands) in magnetic materials, which is highly relevant for engineering quantum states.
